t: EDUCATION: Forgetting Is a Prerequisite for Memory
q: Psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork describe this as the difference between retrieval strength and storage strength. Retrieval strength is how easily you can access something right now. Storage strength is how well it is actually learned and retained over time.

Re-reading a page feels familiar, so it seems like you know it. Watching a clear explanation feels like understanding, but the speaker is carrying the thinking. Even polished AI answers can give the illusion that you've mastered something, when you've only recognized it.
The problem isn't that you forget. It's that you expect not to.
Struggle only helps if it's at the right level. If something is so hard that you have no idea where to start, your working memory gets overloaded and learning breaks down.
Learning happens when you engage with what you can't yet do or recall. That process often feels uncertain or uncomfortable.
x: Bjork retrieval/storage strength distinction: high retrieval strength right now does not equal durable storage strength later -- fluency is misleading.

t: EDUCATION: Beyond the Chatbot, Beyond Efficiency
q: We have become used to talking about AI in terms of efficiency. Chatbots can produce work quickly and often competently, leading us to focus on questions of how much time AI does and does not save us.

Vibecoding with AI makes us all app developers. Agentic AI allows us to assign AI tasks to complete autonomously with minimal oversight. Wearable AI puts on our bodies AI that listens, observes, and captures our surroundings in real time.

A society that produces standardized minds -- minds shaped by the same scope and sequence, evaluated by the same rubric, certified by the same credential -- is producing exactly the population AI is best at substituting for. The factory model is not a defense against AI. The factory model is what AI is replacing.

Blue books and proctored exams and browser lockdown apps are interventions designed for chatbots. These researchers ask us to consider what assessment should look like when generative AI is on our bodies at all times.

t: The Philosophy of Breaking People Down Before Building Them Up

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Why the 'Conceptual Understanding' Debate Is Arguing Over the Wrong Premise
q: A concept is a mental category, a class of objects, symbols or events that share common, defining characteristics. Concept learning has occurred when a student can look at a completely novel, unseen instance and correctly identify whether it belongs in that category or not based on its attributes.
The common error in progressive pedagogy is trying to teach a concept by turning the explanation into a mandatory, step-by-step procedure. I call this the 'proceduralisation' of concepts.

If you force a student to draw a specific bar model, a rectangle or a fraction wall every single time they solve a problem, you have not taught the concept. You have simply taught a drawing algorithm.

We do not test a concept by asking students to define the concept or to reproduce a familiar diagram they saw on the whiteboard. Those are simply verbal or motor algorithms that can be memorised and regurgitated on cue.
Procedural fluency and conceptual understanding are different cognitive architectures. Both matter. Both require instructional designs built for their specific demands.

If the term 'understanding' continues to blur our thinking, we can set it aside and speak directly about concepts, procedures and the behaviours that demonstrate each. Once we do, the debate becomes far less mysterious and the path to better teaching becomes far easier to see.

t: EDUCATION | 5.25.26 Too Many A's, Too Few A-'s
q: A letter grade is, by design, a maximally lossy compression operator. It takes some underlying field of student performance — a semester's worth of papers, exams, participation, problem sets, each themselves already compressions of something else — and projects it onto an ordinal scale with five points (or eleven, counting pluses and minuses).

An A means something to the extent that not-A is a live possibility for the student receiving it. When 85 percent of grades are A-range, the letter A has lost its ordinal information because there's no longer a meaningful 'not-A' to contrast against.

If you take the phrase at face value and ask what qualitative content a letter grade actually carries, the honest answer is: none. What a letter grade carries is a position in a distribution — and the entire signaling value of that position depends on the distribution having dispersion.

Percentile rank reintroduces the dispersion that the letter compression destroyed. Which means the committee's actual diagnosis, stripped of the courage-and-rigor diction, is something like: the letter grade is a bad instrument for the comparative-ranking purpose we've been pretending it serves.

t: Date published: May 24, 2026 No, Explicit Instruction Does Not Cause Learned Helplessness
q: In education, the worry about explicit instruction is most often a general, informal one: that students who receive a great deal of teacher guidance will become passive, over-reliant, and unable to think for themselves. Call this the learner dependence concern. It is a real pedagogical worry.

The concept originated in the work of psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in the 1960s. In a now-famous series of experiments, animals exposed to unavoidable negative outcomes eventually stopped trying to escape even when escape later became possible. The researchers concluded that the animals had learned something powerful: their actions did not matter.

Albert Bandura's research on self-efficacy (1997) documents the opposite pattern clearly: learners develop persistence and confidence when they experience mastery through structured, achievable success. In other words, success builds agency. Repeated failure, especially early, unguided failure, erodes it.

The problem is that the term is frequently misapplied. Once we understand what learned helplessness actually is, and how it actually develops, the claim that explicit instruction produces it becomes very difficult to sustain. In fact, the conditions that give rise to learned helplessness in classrooms are often the opposite of what well-designed explicit instruction creates.

In other words, the goal of explicit instruction is not permanent dependence on the teacher, but to provide enough support early on that students can build the competencies necessary for independent practice.

But the stronger claim — that explicit instruction produces learned helplessness in the clinical sense — does not hold up. Learned helplessness is produced by the repeated experience of trying and failing regardless of effort. That experience is far more likely in classrooms where students are left to grapple with complex ideas without the background knowledge to do so productively.

Well-designed explicit instruction, by contrast, is specifically structured to ensure that students experience success, build accurate knowledge, and develop the confidence that comes from knowing that effort leads to results. It does not produce the conditions for learned helplessness. It prevents them.

Teachers should feel confident using explicit instruction — especially when introducing new material to novice learners — without apology, and without the worry that clarity is somehow doing students a disservice. The path to independent thinking runs through being well taught, not around it.

q: The core mechanic in critical chain project management is almost provocatively simple. You take your team's estimates, cut them all by 50%, and call these new numbers 'aggressive but achievable.' t: The Anticlimax of Achieving a Big Goal
q: Pursuit creates momentum and meaning. Working toward something big gives the everyday structure and focus. People depend on that purpose to summon the discipline and energy to keep going.

Anticipation is often more emotionally intense than possession. Wanting something often produces more stimulation than having it. The chase generates uncertainty, excitement, and optimism. It gives buoyancy to the day-to-day.

People report feeling lethargic, depressed, and lost. Recovery from that emotional flatline usually takes days, sometimes weeks. All of this from actually achieving a big goal that required tremendous sacrifice and effort.
Achievements, even big ones, rarely resolve the deeper human need to imagine a brighter future. With the distraction of pursuit gone, the challenges of the present become more visible.

After the organizing force of a prized goal disappears, strong-minded leaders acknowledge the numbness and admit how depleted they are mentally, emotionally, socially, and physically. They reconnect with the parts of their lives they have neglected and discover value in unstructured time.
Fulfillment, as it turns out, is less about an endpoint and more about ongoing engagement. It is the pursuit of a grand goal, not its attainment, that feeds the spirit.

q: Schools are complex. There are multiple agents interacting and influencing each other in ways that vary in how predictable they are, how desirable they are and how proximal the effects are seen.

Schools improve when children develop academically, socially, emotionally and much much more. At the heart of an improvement model is therefore maximising the chances that children will learn what we intend and make the most of opportunities for incidental learning in all sorts of domains too.

To make the most of these informal opportunities, it becomes vital that there is a shared language for talking about problems, priorities and strategies so a school improvement model must plan for how the team talks, not only because it allows more meaningful collaboration but because changing how we talk changes how we think and if we are to help colleagues to get better, we have to target their beliefs.

t: Levels of Work in School Improvement
q: We define priorities, write plans, agree actions and monitor progress. It gives shape to the work and reassures us that improvement is being organised. But it does embed an assumption about where improvement sits even though it doesn't unfold in a tidy way.

At one end sits change work. This is the work of defining the system within which improvement is supposed to happen. It includes strategic intent, priorities, curriculum design, pedagogical approaches, the way we describe quality.

When these questions are not settled deliberately, they are carried by individuals, often in the moment, often under pressure and often inconsistently. Serve work shapes the conditions under which run work happens. It embeds longer term judgement into the system so that others can act coherently without having to recreate that judgement each time.

Activity can be high while improvement remains uneven. Expectations can be clear while consistency remains difficult. Monitoring can be regular without revealing the reasons behind variation. The same strategy can be introduced across a school and take hold in very different ways.
Planning for emergence means shifting attention upstream, away from refining actions and success criteria, and towards the conditions that shape how people interpret and respond to the work.

When this work is underdeveloped, the system fills the gaps itself. Teachers interpret the curriculum in different ways. Middle leaders construct their own versions of what good looks like. Teams respond to problems locally, drawing on what is available to them.

In complex systems, improvement depends on how consistently judgment is applied across the system and how much variation is designed for rather than accidental -- not on plan clarity.

t: High Expectations, High Support
q: Forty percent of their pupils are classified as vulnerable. Ninety-seven percent are on track in phonics. Those two facts do not coexist by accident. They coexist because someone decided that the second fact was not contingent on the first.
The discovery bags go home from nursery. Not Year 1, not Reception -- nursery. Because the vocabulary gap does not wait for formal schooling to open, and neither should the school.

The workshops make explicit what many schools leave implicit: here is what phonics learning looks like, here is what you are listening for, here is what you can do at home tonight. That is not a soft add-on. That is closing a support gap.

Equity in this school does not mean adjusting expectations downward for children who arrive with less. It means adjusting support upward until the expectation is achievable. The bar stays. The scaffold changes.

Ten to fifteen minutes a day, consistently. That is the finding. Not an intervention programme, not an expensive purchase, not a structural overhaul. Consistent, focused reading practice, every day. The compound effect over a year is larger than most teachers intuitively believe.

Equity is achieved by removing barriers rather than lowering the bar: the standard stays constant and the support varies, which is the inversion of deficit-model accommodation.

t: Do You Even Know What Youre Defending
q: The things they're defending -- the essays, the exams, the rigor, the ritual, and all the other artifacts of the system they deem as possibly imperfect, but by no means broken -- are products of a system designed specifically contrary to human flourishing.

1641 -- Rene Descartes, Netherlands. Sitting alone in a heated room by candlelight, he decides the mind and body are fundamentally separate substances. I think, therefore I am. Not, I have a family, therefore I am. Not I love my dog, therefore I am.

Adam Smith visits a pin factory -- the needle for industrial sewing machines -- and sees the average person make 20 pins. Then he visits another factory and watches workers produce 48,000 pins a day by dividing the job into eighteen specialized steps. He goes home and writes The Wealth of Nations. Fragment any human activity into its smallest parts and optimize each one. Schools will absorb this logic fifty years later.

Prussian generals are sitting by candlelight trying to understand how Napoleon destroyed their entire army in a single afternoon. Their conclusion: our soldiers ran because they lacked obedience and loyalty to the state. Their solution: build compulsory schools. The factory model of education is born as a military project.

Ten university presidents, chaired by Harvard's president, convene to decide what every American child should learn -- based on what universities want for admissions. They fragment human knowledge into siloed subjects divided by bells. The academic hierarchy that still governs schools today is decided in a single meeting.

Cognition as what it means to be human. Everything that happens after this, intentionally or otherwise, takes this idea as its lead. And the consequence is that everything we do in Western culture is designed to maximize the efficiency by which information gets put into the brain.

q: Here we see that only 5% of full-time teachers are working for the amount of hours they are contractually paid for in their salary. That's not to say the workload of all teachers isn't high. However, as a profession we often aren't the best at putting measures in place to make our lives easier.

There is a perception that it is a teachers autonomy to plan and teach a class the way they feel comfortable, and to a degree that is true. As I've argued before though, autonomy doesn't come from creating the resources yourself, they come from how you inject your own personality and flair to bring them to life.

Meanwhile leaders are spending around 50% of their time in meetings which while important a lot of the time can mean they spend more time discussing rather than acting on school priorities and making the impact they ideally dreamed of when becoming a leader.

One question I always ask when planning a meeting is 'Could a staff member passively exist in this meeting and leave without needing to act on anything?'. t: The Problem With Always Having the Answer
q: I'm not stepping in because they need me to, but because watching them struggle with something makes me uncomfortable. My control pattern activates. What I tell myself is that I'm teaching them or showing them a better way. But what I'm actually doing is managing my own discomfort while robbing them of the opportunity to learn.

These patterns have nothing to do with the people we lead and everything to do with us -- our need for control, our discomfort with uncertainty or disorder, and our desire to feel valuable. When we provide answers instead of developing capability, we create costs for both our team and ourselves.

There's a principle I've noticed repeatedly in leadership, which I refer to as pattern inversion: The space we occupy as leaders is the space our team learns to vacate. When we occupy the space of solving, rescuing, and providing answers, our team slowly vacates the space of critical thinking, ownership, and problem-solving.

Create the conditions for success. Provide the tools, direction, support, and boundaries. Then step back and let people learn through the process -- even when it's slower, messier, or different than how you would do it.

Leadership is about creating the conditions for independence while building an environment where people can collaboratively develop confidence, judgment, and capability over time. Yes, this is harder in the short term. It takes longer, and it's messier.

t: Instructional Fidelity: The Price of Certainty
q: Scripted phonics is what you get when an evidence regime that demands fidelity to a protocol meets a political body that demands certainty, peace of mind. This has nothing to do with science; science rejects certainty and demands falsifiability. The script isn't primarily a pedagogical artifact. It is a fidelity-delivery mechanism.

A mandated curriculum or a scripted program allows politicians to declare they have 'solved' the problem without having to do the targeted work of training and supporting teachers as professional learners and practitioners or addressing underlying inequities.

Teachers pay a severe cost for second-hand certainty: their authority to interpret empirical research for themselves is denied, and their license to respond to the complexities of the classroom is revoked. Medical researchers do not write protocols that interchangeable practitioners read verbatim. They write guidelines that credentialed clinicians interpret in light of the patient and the patient's circumstances.

Scripts and fidelity protocols are written for substitute teachers. Deviation is reframed as infidelity and used to invalidate the intervention's effect. The teacher who reads the child in front of them is, by the regime's own grammar, the contaminating variable.

Medicine uses evidence as a floor for practice. Most children do need phonics instruction to varying degrees in particular contexts. That's a floor. Scripted phonics uses evidence as a ceiling. Fidelity is the price of feeling certain. Judgment is the price of being relevant.

The cost is paid by the six-year-old who is already feeling and falling behind, and by the songbird in seventh-grade English who loves to read series books and has not yet been taught what to do with a page that resists easy resolution.

t: How to Stop Looking Weak on Stage in 9 Minutes

When you shrink your body, make nervous movements, and avoid eye contact, you are silently communicating to the world that you do not trust your own worth and that you are willing to be dominated.

A gaze that rests on people instead of sliding past them. Shoulders that hold their natural width without performing height. Hands that have somewhere to be. A voice that takes up its share of the room without forcing. A walk that arrives.

t: Frankly Speaking, Frank Smith Is Wrong to Treat Reading as a Biologically Primary Skill
q: Once Smith commits to viewing reading as similar to speaking because they are both 'bringing sense to meaningful situations' with 'very little additional effort required to use the eyes,' he straps himself into an instructional straightjacket that prevents acknowledgment of the importance of teaching foundational skills to facilitate access to print.

I am not suggesting that Frank Smith has nothing to say about reading. On the contrary, his emphasis on the importance of meaning-making is significant. I am merely siding with the science when it comes to helping children crack the alphabetic code because there's a reality I cannot alter: my students are wired for sound, not for print.

Alphabetic print is a cultural invention, not a natural biological adaptation. Spoken language arrives already phonologically available to the listener; print does not. Mapping visual symbols onto speech is not merely using the eyes instead of the ears; it requires learning an artificial code.

Context supports comprehension, but it cannot substitute for the development of precise print recognition. Thus, biologically primary skills are acquired implicitly, rapidly, and without formal instruction. By contrast, biologically secondary skills are acquired slowly, effortfully, and typically only through explicit teaching.

What I didn't know when my whole-language colleague and I swapped books -- and what I have only recently discovered -- is David Geary's distinction between biologically primary and biologically secondary knowledge. Since becoming familiar with this distinction, however, I believe it tells me all I need to know about where Smith went wrong in his thinking.

t: Why Predators Thrive in Rule-Heavy Systems
q: Most people assume that more rules create safer organizations. Often, the opposite is true. Some of the most psychologically unsafe, ethically compromised, and structurally abusive environments are not chaotic organizations with no governance at all. They are highly regulated systems overflowing with policies, procedures, bylaws, compliance protocols, reporting structures, and credentialing requirements.

From the predator's point of view, if a box was checked, a meeting was held, a committee approved something, or a policy was technically followed, integrity has been preserved -- they cannot be called out. Good people are often genuinely confused by this behavior, because they would never think to use the rules that way.

Research by organizational psychologist Gerhard Blickle and colleagues found that Machiavellian individuals with strong political skill are often rated favorably by coworkers and supervisors even while engaging in self-serving or harmful conduct. Skillful manipulation looks like professionalism to people who aren't as slick. Expertise in working the rules becomes protective cover.

In many dioceses, allegations were routed through internal review systems, personnel procedures, legal processes, and hierarchical reporting structures that appeared orderly on paper -- while those same systems prioritized institutional preservation over vulnerable individuals. As abusive priests were moved from one diocese to the next, the system was functioning as designed.

Highly procedural systems disproportionately reward individuals with unusually high appetites for control, conflict endurance, and strategic manipulation. Healthy, empathic professionals generally enter organizations to build, solve problems, and contribute meaningfully. They typically assume others are operating in good faith. Manipulative individuals operate differently.

The same pattern appeared in the Larry Nassar case. Athletes, parents, trainers, and medical professionals raised concerns repeatedly. Within a highly credentialed sports and medical bureaucracy, those complaints were minimized, redirected, or procedurally managed. The institutional structure protected the abuser.

Leaders look like they are playing favorites when they hold some team members' feet to the fire while letting others spin out of control. This undermines the team, the culture, and overall performance.

t: Why Do Leaders Tolerate Poor Performers
q: Tolerating poor performers is a common failure for far too many leaders. Inexplicably, leaders and managers who know better cover for weak performers and offer a wide variety of rationalizations for doing so.

Many leaders want to avoid conflict and dislike difficult conversations. They find that giving candid feedback and working through low performance can be emotionally draining, so problems get postponed.
Other leaders remember when the team member was strong and showed potential, and they are not ready to give up on that image. They keep waiting for a turnaround that usually never arrives.

A recent study of human resources executives found they trust less than 40 percent of leaders and managers to hold poor performers accountable. A separate study found the second most common reason boards fire a CEO is for tolerating poor performance -- not far behind weak long-term company performance.
High performers often leave the team in disgust, believing excellence is undermined when leaders tolerate incompetence.
When leaders refuse to address poor performance, bystanders and stakeholders lose confidence and trust in them.
Rationalizations for avoiding the need to address the poor performer are legion. But good leaders never excuse weak performance. They tackle it head-on.

t: Two Small Secrets To Cold Call Success
q: Dave gives his students a bit of time to write brief responses to a poem they've just read. Then he says: 'How many people have at least one idea down?' Students raise their hands. 'Great. Keep your hands up if you have at least two ideas down.'

He's basically said: 'Who has an answer or an idea right now?' When students raise their hands, it's now doubly-easy to call on them. 'Great. Juan tell us what you wrote about...' Dave here starts with Kamari and it's easy to do because she's already signalled to him that she's thought productively about the question and has ideas.

After Kamari gives her answer, Dave says, 'How many people had something like that?' Lots of kids raise their hands. The result is that Kamari instantly sees that people thought similarly and agreed with her. Dave is amplifying her perception of peer agreement and approval and this is very powerful as it makes her feel successful after responding, like she added something valid to the discussion.

It's good if Dave says, 'Hmmm, Kamari, what a good idea,' but we know that a student's perception of her peers' approval is much more influential. Dave is making that approval more legible to her: Look at all the people who agree with you!

I use a version of this move all the time with adult participants in professional development, and I especially rely on two Norm Amplification phrases that I think are eminently copy-able. After someone gives an answer I say: 'Hmm. I see lots of people nodding their heads' or 'Hmmm. I see lots of people writing that down.'

In both cases I am merely drawing the speaker's attention to the fact that other people in the room valued what they said, and this is a strong incentive to speak again and to believe, accurately, that they added value.
Once you have that signal: I've thought about it; I have an opinion, the Cold Call feels doubly inviting. This makes the Cold Call feel natural, conversational and inclusive.

t: Trauma induced teaching isn't unique
q: What struck me is that what a student with trauma needs corresponds one-to-one with what every student needs, namely, good instruction in a psychologically safe environment. Of course, different children with different needs need more of one thing and less of another, but the principles remain the same. Good instruction is good instruction.

Learning spaces should be stand-alone classrooms, not open-plan environments with inadequate sound dampening and constant visual distraction from other classrooms. Children should be seated in rows, facing the teacher when they are being taught new knowledge and skills.
Classrooms should be calm, orderly and predictable learning spaces, as a reflection of taught behaviour expectations and adult-led limit-setting with clear, consistent and fair consequences.
Instruction should be educator-led. Educators take responsibility for the teaching of new content. This is not left to chance via discovery learning.

Device use is minimal to non-existent. Except in timetabled IT classes, technology has little to no intrinsic learning benefit in classrooms. Pseudoscientific tools and practices are not in use (e.g., Learning Styles / Multiple Intelligences Inventories; Brain Gym; Whole Language/Balanced Literacy approaches to reading instruction; discovery learning for maths).

Non-volunteers are called on (so-called 'cold-calling' – better described as 'warm calling') to respond to carefully framed questions about material that has been taught. This ensures that all children participate in classroom learning, with adjustments and accommodations if needed, to support this.

t: The Visualiser: The Complete Guide
q: A visualiser is a mounted document camera that projects whatever sits beneath it onto a screen or whiteboard in real time. Unlike modelling at a whiteboard, it allows the teacher to face the class throughout. Eye contact and monitoring never stop and the classroom stays in view.

The most powerful use is showing the work in progress, not the polished product. A mini-whiteboard placed under the visualiser is the ideal modelling surface. It's erasable, so the teacher can revise, cross out, and redo in real time. The impermanence is the point because students see that thinking is revisable, not fixed.

Barak Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction are closely aligned with the practice of visualising work live in the classroom. The principles emphasise presenting new material in small steps, providing worked examples, and demonstrating what success looks like before students attempt independent practice.

John Sweller's research established that working memory is limited and easily overwhelmed. When students have to simultaneously decode verbal instructions, imagine a visual layout, and recall content knowledge, cognitive load can become unmanageable. The visualiser reduces that load by making one element -- the layout and process -- perceptually available rather than imagined.

When a teacher narrates aloud while modelling under a visualiser -- 'I'm going to write my topic sentence here, and I'm going to keep it to one sentence, not two, because...' -- students receive information simultaneously through verbal and visual channels. Research on dual coding by Allan Paivio and later work by Richard E. Mayer suggests that learning becomes more durable when words and visuals are meaningfully combined.

Place a strong response under the visualiser (with the student's permission, or anonymised). Talk through what makes it effective. Then place a response with a common error and model the correction live. Students annotate their own work as you go.

Doug Lemov calls a version of this Show Call -- picking up a student's work mid-task and projecting it without warning. The accountability effect is significant: when students know any piece of work might go under the camera, the quality of independent practice changes.

t: School Improvement 201: What to Actually Do With Your Summer
q: Summer is not for more dreaming. Summer is for translating those OKRs into systems, systems into behaviors, and behaviors into milestones with dates on them. That's the gap between a design and an implementation — and it's where almost every school improvement plan quietly dies.

You agreed on what. You never agreed on how. Or who. Or by when. You set a goal to move proficiency, and never decided which three teacher behaviors actually move it, who's responsible for installing them, and what they should look like by the second week versus the second month.

A plan is not an implementation. An OKR is not a system. And a leadership team that has dreamed together but not built together is a team that will improvise once the building fills up — and improvisation, at scale, across thirty adults and four hundred kids, is just chaos with good intentions.
The whole job of the summer is to make September boring. Predictable. Designed.

Buy-in doesn't come from a poster. It comes from clarity plus competence — from teachers walking in knowing exactly what the culture is, what it looks like when they do it, and feeling ready to deliver it the same way the teacher next door will.

A leadership team should leave the summer able to answer one question instantly, in unison: when this system breaks in October, who handles it and how? If you get blank stares, you have more summer work to do.

t: From AI Tutors to AI Study Mates
q: Students were split into three groups: one had access to a standard ChatGPT-4 interface ('GPT Base'), one had access to a version with teacher-designed guardrails that gave hints rather than answers ('GPT Tutor'), and a control group had only textbook and notes. During the practice sessions, the AI groups crushed it. The GPT Base group performed a whopping 48% better than the control group.

Then, the researchers took the AI away and gave everyone an exam. The students who had used the unguarded GPT Base performed 17% worse on the exam than the control group who had never had AI access at all.
TLDR: AI tutors didn't help students to learn -- it helped them to perform.
AI tutors tend to be optimised for task completion and actively undermine the processes through which durable learning happens.

The LLMs entering education and training were not built for education or training -- they were built for work. The logic that makes them useful at work -- optimise the output, minimise cognitive effort, treat each interaction as disposable -- is precisely what makes them unsuitable as learning tools.

Yan, Greiff, Lodge and Gasevic (2025) put it bluntly in Nature Reviews Psychology: we're confusing performance gains with learning. In practice, this means every 'AI improved completion rates by 40%' pitch you've been getting this year is potentially measuring the exact outcome that doesn't matter.

t: A Powerful Truth: How Displays Of Strength Project Weakness
q: A player with a poor hand will bet as though they have a sure thing, hoping to trick the other players into folding. The truth is that the player who attempts to bluff always does so from a position of deficiency. You wouldn't be bluffing if you placed a high bet on, say, a straight or a flush unless you somehow knew for a fact that your opponent held four of a kind. Therefore, bluffing is always a de facto admission of weakness even when the bluff works and the player wins.

Bullies never pick fights they don't think they can win. When they become adults, we call this 'punching down.' The whole point is to look tough, not to actually be tough—similar to a poker bluff. Bullying behavior exposes the true coward lurking beneath the aggression.

The bigger the parade, the frailer the leadership. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union was famous for its large military displays featuring a slow procession of tanks, missiles, and other armaments punctuating endless columns of synchronized soldiers. While an impressive sight and more than a little intimidating, the world knew that Soviet leaders relied on such spectacles to distract from their failures.

Bigwigs who bluster and boast are compensating for some shortcoming or other—real or imagined. No matter how successful the boss, you can bet that their tough-guy act is a cover for their lack of confidence.
Leaders don't have to show off because they have the intestinal fortitude to act with humility.

True leaders understand not to make choices that cut down, belittle, or oppress their team members. If—being human—they ever slip and fall for the trappings of power, they then will admit their error and correct accordingly.

t: The Metaphor that Changed Everything
q: In the 1950s, psychologists started to notice something remarkable: computers and the human mind can be measured in very similar ways. They both process information that can be measured in 'bits'. He discovered something mathematical about the human brain.

Norbert Wiener noticed that the human mind constantly makes predictions and corrections without effort. In designing his weapon, he noticed something remarkable: The machine needed to use the same loop: goal, action, outcome, correction. It didn't matter if it was a machine or a human brain; the process was the same.
A powerful new metaphor was born: mind-as-computer. The idea wasn't to understand why the brain works as it does, but how to observe and measure what it does.

For the first time, a computer program was shown to mimic the invisible processes of the mind. This work established a fundamentally new way to think about, test, and understand the mind using the rigor of mathematics and computer programming.

t: How to Become Someone People Trust (Building Trust Part 3)
q: Nobody says I don't trust you in a professional context. Instead, people stay quiet in meetings. They handle things themselves rather than asking for help. They stop advocating for you when you're not in the room. The absence of trust produces a feeling of friction, of distance, of energy that isn't quite converting into results, but it rarely produces a conversation.

Trust is what moves your career. Even more than your competence or your output. When people decide to give you an opportunity, recommend you when you're not present, defend your decisions when they come under pressure — they are acting from a felt sense of trust. Trust is the invisible air in your sails.

Charles Feltman's work identifies four components that, taken together, determine whether another person experiences you as trustworthy: sincerity (you mean what you say), reliability (you do what you say), competence (you can do what you say), and care (the other person believes you have their interests at heart, not just your own agenda).

You can be sincere, reliable, and competent and still be mistrusted, if the people around you sense they are instruments of your goals rather than people you genuinely care about. This is the care deficit, and it is remarkably common among high-performing mid-level leaders who have been rewarded primarily for delivery.

Trust isn't a conclusion people reach by reasoning; it's a response they have to how it feels to be with you. This matters because it means trust is not primarily a strategy. It is the outcome of a practice. And like any practice, it can be trained.

t: The Instructional Hierarchy
q: Acquisition: Students learn math facts by connecting new facts to what they already know. The goal is to answer accurately but using a range of strategies, without an emphasis on speed.
In the acquisition stage, timed practice isn't appropriate. The goal is to get students calculating accurately and connecting what they're learning to what they already know.

This is the core challenge of fact fluency. If I'm working with a student one-on-one, the instructional hierarchy is really useful! In a classroom with a wide range of students, the reality is much more complicated.
Repetitive practice is most useful when students are in the fluency stage. Asking students to practice something while they are still in the acquisition stage is going to be inefficent.

I've seen this over and over again: students are trying to practice something but their working memory is overwhelmed, their work is slow and error-prone, the practice isn't very productive, and the whole experience is unpleasant for students.

t: Reading Big Words: What It Looks Like in the Classroom, the School, and the State
q: It was a coherent picture of what this work looks like when it's done with intention, at every level of the system.
From the Classroom: Faith Howard, Wyoming Faith Howard is a 6-12 literacy interventionist and specialist in rural Wyoming, with a background as a high school English teacher.
Her message was simple and urgent: decoding alone is only half the equation.

Faith has built her intervention work around the reciprocal relationship between encoding and decoding -- the idea that orthographic mapping doesn't fully happen unless students are also learning to spell and write the words they're learning to read.

She pulls directly from the texts her students are reading that week -- novels like Just Mercy or The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks -- choosing words that are tier two or tier three, morphologically rich, and essential for comprehending, discussing, and writing about the text.

She cross-references those words against a diagnostic spelling screener to identify patterns where her students are struggling, then groups the words accordingly to double-dip on both pronunciation and spelling instruction.
On Mondays, students work through word pyramids -- isolating each syllable of a word, building up slowly, with bonus questions about vowel variability.

Most of us were carrying over 100lbs including our packs, body armor, and weapon systems, but depending on the specific job (rifleman, machine-gunner, mortar-man) some were carrying much more.
Early mornings in Southern California's coastal mountains are beautiful and fragrant with chapparal, and we saw many--probably all of them--during our time in training to become infantrymen.

We all knew that the next several hours would be physically miserable.

t: You Are Not Your Personality Test

The instructional principle Palincsar and Brown articulated was deceptively simple. The teacher relinquishes the task to the novice only at the level the novice can negotiate at this moment. As the novice becomes more competent, the teacher increases her demands -- one stage further into the zone of proximal development.

A lethal mutation is a change that preserves the surface features of the original -- the parts that are visible, namable, and easy to operationalize -- while destroying the interior mechanism that made the original work. The mutated version looks like the thing, but superficially. And because it looks like the thing, the people implementing it cannot tell that they have lost what mattered.

By the end of the three steps, what was happening in classrooms labeled 'reciprocal teaching' had no functional resemblance to what Palincsar and Brown had done in 1984. The surface features were all present. The four strategies were taught and practiced. Students took turns. The teacher modeled and faded. But reciprocal teaching was gone.

The reciprocal teaching being implemented was a fluent execution of the observable features of the 1984 study, conducted in the complete absence of the thing the 1984 study was about. This is what makes the mutation lethal rather than merely incomplete.

An innovation that works has to scale, scaling means going to teachers who were not part of its development, those teachers need materials, materials require specification, specification favors the observable over the interior, the observable features get codified, the codification becomes the program, and the program is what fidelity is measured against.

Notice what this is not. It is not a prompt-engineering curriculum. It is not a set of rules for using AI responsibly. It is not a worksheet with boxes labeled Question, Summarize, Clarify, Predict. The moment it becomes any of those things, it has been lethally mutated, and we are back at the macrorules with a different label on the anchor chart.

The teacher who can do this work is doing the same work Palincsar's teachers were doing with Sara in 1984 -- hosting a novice inside a discourse she is gradually internalizing, increasing the demands one stage further into the zone of proximal development as the novice becomes capable of more.

t: How Talk Does Things in Schools
q: Walk into any school and almost everything you observe is downstream of talk. Teachers build curriculum in planning meetings. Principals shape culture through the phrases they repeat. Students learn to think by speaking before they write. We tend to treat conversation as the setting in which educational work happens. It might be more accurate to say it is the work.

The default assumption is that talk transmits ideas — that meaning travels from one mind to another like a document passed across a table. Meaning is not transferred. It is built, jointly, in the live act of speaking and responding.

The word "rigor" means something different to the department chair than to the new teacher across the table. "Student-centered" carries one mental model for one person and something else entirely for another. The conversation feels productive. The shared ground isn't actually there.

A department meeting where everyone shares ideas but no one makes a clear request is not just an inefficient meeting — it is a meeting where talk, for all its apparent activity, did nothing. No action was generated. No commitment was taken.
What this body of work ultimately argues is that talk in schools needs to be understood as a technical practice, not just a social one.
It is not enough to create space for talk. The question is whether the talk being done is the kind that builds shared ground, generates real commitment, and moves people toward action.

t: Why Orwell Still Matters: Reason 3621
q: My student didn't arrive at his interpretive confidence on his own. It was given to him by a school culture that has absorbed, in diluted and well-intentioned form, the postmodern turn in literary theory. The message, transmitted not as doctrine but as atmosphere, is something like: your response to a text is inherently valid. Meaning lives in the reader. There are no wrong answers, only under-explored ones.

It doesn't free the student from authority. It insulates him from the discomfort of being wrong, dresses that insulation in the language of epistemology, and hands it to him as a gift from the institution. He now carries institutional permission to dismiss any reading that ranks above his own.

Postmodern relativism in schools was never really philosophy. It was a permission structure. And like all permission structures, it serves the institution at least as much as the student. A classroom where all interpretations are equal is a classroom where no one fails, no one is uncomfortable, and no difficult conversation about evidence and warrant ever quite lands.

Orwell was not a relativist. He was a radical empiricist who believed that seeing clearly was a moral act, not merely an intellectual preference. The through-line is the same: the refusal to let the institution pre-answer the question. The Ministry of Truth's deepest crime wasn't lying. It was destroying the capacity to care about the difference.

That capacity is precisely what a certain strain of well-meaning pedagogy has been quietly eroding. Not through malice. Through comfort. Through the slow institutional preference for students who feel validated over students who have been genuinely challenged.
If he reads 1984 and comes away more committed to the idea that no external standard of truth exists, did the book fail? Or did the institution succeed?

t: When 'Evidence-Based' Starts Meaning Everything... and Nothing
q: Research-based is the more modest claim. A programme described as research-based may have drawn on existing research findings during its development, but drawing on research is not the same as being shown to work. A literacy programme might reference research on oral language, motivation, or the value of discussion... while still having no independent evidence that the programme itself improves reading outcomes.

In practice, research-based has become one of the most overused and least scrutinised phrases in literacy education. It is often applied so broadly, and with so little consistency, that it can function as a kind of all-purpose defence, a way of claiming a relationship with research without being held accountable to any particular standard of evidence.

The language of research can sound extremely persuasive, particularly when wrapped in polished presentations, confident delivery, and references to 'brain science'. Part of teachers' professional responsibility is learning to pause and ask: what kind of evidence actually sits underneath this claim? How strong is it? And does the confidence of the messaging match the quality of the evidence being presented?

The conclusion that systematic, explicit phonics instruction works is not the same thing as saying that every programme marketed as a phonics programme is equally effective. Some phonics programmes have been independently evaluated through rigorous research and produce reliable outcomes for children. Others are more accurately described as research-based.

Snake oil relies on persuasive marketing, compelling testimonials, and grand promises rather than robust proof. Literacy education is not immune to this. Programmes can appear highly scientific through the use of neuroscience terminology, selective citations, and references to 'brain-based learning', even where the evidential foundations are weak, incomplete, or contested.

'It worked in our school' is not the same thing as evidence that something works, and conflating the two is where the field has repeatedly run into difficulty. Professional experience matters. But we need to be precise about what kind of claim is being made and what level of evidence supports it.

Reading is not simply another school subject. It is the gateway through which children access almost everything else in education. Teachers who understand what these terms actually mean, and who feel comfortable to ask what kind of evidence is really on the table, are better placed to make decisions that genuinely serve the children in front of them.

t: Too Fast, Too Confident, Too Digital?
q: When students read digitally, they read faster, became more overconfident, and understood less. This isn't a small educational detail. It's a flashing RED warning light.

Salomon introduced the idea of Amount of Invested Mental Effort, which he defined as the number of nonautomatic mental elaborations learners apply to material. In other words: not how much effort the task objectively demands, but how much effort the learner actually chooses to put in. And that distinction matters enormously.

Digital reading feels easier, and because it feels easier, students invest less effort reading it. They glide through the text, don't pause, don't reread, don't test themselves, and don't notice confusion. They mistake fluency for understanding; metacognition gone wrong.

Students reading digitally weren't only understanding less; they were also more confident that they'd understood what they had read. They suffer from a variation of the Dunning-Kruger effect and can be seen as the educational equivalent of driving faster in fog while believing visibility has improved.

Why are they reading this text digitally in the first place? This sounds almost too simple, and that's why it'll probably be ignored. In education, we have a habit of creating problems and then designing interventions to solve the problems we've created.

Screens are associated with scrolling, chatting, searching, watching, gaming, swiping, and grazing. Paper, by contrast, still carries a school-like seriousness. It says: sit down, slow down, this matters.

For sustained reading and understanding of complex material, especially for children and young adolescents still developing the metacognitive skills that they need for independent study, print may reduce unnecessary problems and invite more appropriate effort.

t: The Shadow That Has Your Name
q: Ged nearly dies and for most of the novel he flees it. Eventually he turns around and gives chase instead. The climax is when Ged speaks the shadow's true name, and the name is his own. What had been pursuing him was the unintegrated darkness of his own nature, the part his pride had refused to see. In naming it, he incorporates it and becomes, finally, whole.

Le Guin was deeply influenced by Jungian psychology, and the shadow in the novel is a conscious borrowing. Jung's shadow is everything we have refused to integrate: the capacities we denied, the failures we couldn't acknowledge, the parts of ourselves that pride or fear made unacceptable.

In an educational setting, this shows up in a familiar way: a student who cannot recognise their own confusion often externalises it. The teacher is unclear, the subject is irrelevant, the assessment is unfair. Naming the shadow, in Jung's sense, is the precondition for any genuine development.

Hegel's dialectic moves through negation: you only come to know something fully by encountering what resists or contradicts it. Mastery is the progressive integration of everything that initially resisted you, rather than the accumulation of correct answers. Shortcuts foreclose development: they let you route around the negation rather than through it.

A student who has prompted their way to a polished essay has not encountered their own shadow in the process. The skills worth cultivating now are those that AI cannot perform on a student's behalf: the ability to name things precisely, to recognise your own shadow when it appears, and to stay with it rather than reach for the nearest exit.
Ged cannot outsource his shadow to anyone else. It carries his name. The reckoning has to be personal, or it doesn't happen at all.

t: People Who Didn't Receive Praise as Children
q: People who grew up without receiving much praise have an unusual affliction. They often struggle with compliments as adults. Strangely enough, compliments and praise create real discomfort for them. This isn't false modesty. They often perceive praise and compliments as disingenuous attempts to influence them. Or as superfluous noise.

They learned as children to depend on their own internal validation, praise directed at them doesn't register as psychologically rewarding, as it does for other adults. Unless it perfectly matches their own internal accounting, praise and compliments are viewed as words without much value.

The best way to encourage a praise-allergic team member isn't through general praise or enthusiastic compliments. It's through observation. Observational praise and compliments cut through the noise and positively influence these team members in the same way general praise works with everyone else.

'You did an amazing job' doesn't register, but 'You patiently listened to me when I was agitated' does. The more specific the observation, the better. Specificity contains data that can be cross-checked and run through their internal validation system.
Observation of praise-worthy behavior lands well with all team members, not just those who view praise as uncomfortable and unnecessary.

q: In our school communities, kids need to feel they matter. That they are valuable and valued. That we want them to be there to learn because it's important, interesting stuff. There in person, in front of us, detached from a screen. That every child in a class is heard. That they are welcome and important and safe.

The ever-creeping use of AI as a tool by which students think they 'learn' something is very concerning. For many of them, ChatGPT is a go-to for finding stuff, and thinking they know it. But they're not learning it, and don't know it, and are certainly not questioning it.

Isn't there something hauntingly depressing in this vision of schooling? Something hollowed out and empty and sad? Where is the curriculum that helps children know and argue and challenge and build? Where is the design of a beautiful curriculum so that our children can, in Michael Oakeshott's words, enter into the conversation of mankind?

Rob Henderson argues that affluent people promote luxury beliefs because they know that the adoption of those beliefs will cost them less than others. He argues that luxury beliefs confer status on the upper class... while inflicting costs on the lower classes.

It is this problem that education needs to address and it is a hard problem. We might assume that engaging visuals or a pseudo-intelligent computer program would help children over the motivational hump, but history tells us otherwise. It takes far more -- external motivators that gradually transition to internal motivators as capabilities incrementally increase. Children need to practise things they don't really want to practise.

I remember sitting in that class thinking I had never, ever before felt anything so viscerally when reading a text. That feeling that shook and broke the voice of my 17-year-old self as I read made me feel something bigger than I had ever thought possible: it took me beyond the perimeter of my own life into a different time, space, person and being. It gave me the power of thought that I didn't know I was capable of. And that was beautiful, and enabling, and empowering.

t: Life Under the Parental Eye of Sauron
q: There is alarming research that shows that teens who know their parents are tracking them tend to make poorer decisions when it comes to personal safety. It's as if they abdicate responsibility for themselves, assuming that their parent can always find them and get them out of any sticky situation.

A survey in the Netherlands found that teens whose parents tracked them were more likely to engage in secretive behaviours and provide fewer details about their friends, activities, and social lives than teens whose parents did not track them. It suggests that the more a teen feels their privacy is being invaded, the more they want to hide information, which ultimately backfires on the parent.

By tracking our kids, we're essentially telling them that it is acceptable to surrender their privacy to anyone who claims to love them, whether it's ourselves or their friends or future lovers. And that's not OK!

Now controlling behavior among intimate partners resembles nothing so much as just another day with a helicopter parent, with an expectation that location sharing and read receipts are turned on. Surveillance keeps us all safe, after all. 'It's for your own good!' It's easy to see how parents' behavior has paved the way for demands like these to seem reasonable rather than invasive.

I am disturbed by how normal it has become to keep tabs on everyone's whereabouts, all the time. Parents track kids, kids track parents, spouses track each other; even close friends and adult siblings share locations.
The level of independence they have correlates to their trustworthiness; the more reliable they are, the more leeway they will get.

t: How Can We Improve Teachers?
q: Coaching teachers normally focuses entirely on teaching — it misses 50% of what makes a difference: the curriculum. Curriculum means the tasks, models, explanations, success criteria, retrieval and practice students encounter in the lesson. To ignore this is crazy.

Teaching is king, but curriculum is queen, and she wears the trousers. It doesn't matter how brilliant your teaching is, if your retrieval curriculum doesn't make students remember it, they will learn less.
If you improve an aspect of the curriculum, you improve it for all teachers and all students. So curriculum fixes take precedent over all teaching fixes (except for real behaviour issues).
3 habits are not overwhelming. These habits are easy to acquire, because they are attached to already successful routines. This is habit stacking, a core concept from James Clear's Atomic Habits.

You are focusing on these as a team because this is what is going to lead to the most progress for all your students. Teachers who are brilliant at these are going to help those who aren't yet brilliant. You can rehearse these techniques in a department meeting.

t: From Parts to Patterns: The Mental Tools of Systems Thinking
q: Some problems cannot be understood only by taking them apart. Their behavior comes from relationships, feedback, timing, incentives, assumptions, and interactions. The issue is not always in the parts themselves. Sometimes the issue is in the pattern the parts are creating together.

This is why a solution may work once and fail later. The system has changed in response to the solution. Circular thinking helps us notice feedback. Some feedback reinforces a pattern. The more something happens, the more it continues to happen. Trust builds trust. Mistrust builds mistrust.

Emergence is difficult because it challenges blame. It suggests that outcomes may arise not from one broken part, but from the structure of interaction itself. A group may have capable individuals and still produce confusion. A process may have well-defined steps and still create delays.

Systems thinking should often come before analytical thinking in complex situations. Before we break a problem into pieces, we need some sense of the whole. Without a systems frame, analysis can become fragmentation. We may analyze the wrong parts.

The way we draw the boundary shapes what we can see. Draw the boundary around one task, and the problem may look like execution. Draw it around incentives, and it may look like behavior. Draw it around time, and it may look like a feedback loop. The boundary determines the story.

Systems thinking is often presented as a set of tools: diagrams, maps, loops, models, and frameworks. These tools matter. They help make invisible patterns visible. But before systems thinking becomes a diagram, it is a discipline of attention.

t: Frederick Russell Burnham: The Most Fascinating Man You've Never Heard Of
q: Frederick Russell Burnham lived a life so extraordinary that it seems almost fictional. He was a frontiersman, soldier, explorer, spy, adventurer, oil tycoon, and one of the greatest scouts of his era. Over the course of his remarkable life, Burnham survived deadly campaigns in Africa, tracked enemies across deserts and wilderness, escaped captivity during war, dined with Queen Victoria, advised powerful world leaders, and helped inspire the creation of the Boy Scouts.

His life embodied many of the qualities that people still admire in great adventurers and gentlemen: resilience, competence, bravery, self-reliance, and humble confidence. Simply put, Frederick Russell Burnham lived the kind of life most men only read about in novels, and his story remains one of the most fascinating adventure tales of the modern age.

Baden-Powell even adopted Burnham's style of dress, a Stetson hat and a neckerchief. Their conversations about training boys in fieldcraft and outdoor skills directly inspired Baden-Powell to create the Boy Scouts. Burnham is often called the father of scouting and remained active in the Boy Scouts for the rest of his life.

He was twice captured by the Boers and escaped both times, once by lying motionless in an open field for four days. Later, he was seriously wounded and sent to England to recover. While in London, Burnham received a hero's welcome.

He played a decisive role in ending the conflict by locating and eliminating the Matabele spiritual leader, Mlimo. With fellow scout Bonar Armstrong, Burnham infiltrated a remote cave where Mlimo was hiding and fatally shot him, paving the way for Cecil Rhodes to broker peace.

Despite his wealth, Burnham remained committed to public service and conservation. He was a founding member of the California State Parks Commission, helping to preserve California's natural beauty for future generations.

t: Coaching Cut 51: Over-modelling
q: The pitfall lives in the modelling stage of coaching. The coach stands up, models the action step, and the coachee watches. So far so good. But the coach doesn't stop at the action step. They keep going, modelling what comes next, or what came before, or both. By the time they finish, the coachee has seen a longer sequence of teaching and can't tell where the action step started and stopped.

Over-modelling doesn't happen because coaches are careless. It happens because the bits around the action step feel natural to include. If the action step is about developing a whiteboard routine, it feels logical to also show what you'd do once the boards are up.

The problem is that coaching isn't a real lesson. The model exists to give the coachee a clear, focused image of the thing they are working on. The moment you extend beyond the action step, you dilute that focus.

If you don't have that clarity, what should be a manageable step soon feels like too much. The coachee is now trying to hold two (or three) techniques at once, and the one they're meant to be practising gets lost in the noise.

By isolating the routine, you let the coachee see it clearly, understand why each part matters, and rehearse it without the cognitive load of also thinking about what comes next. The boundary also communicates something important: that this routine is worth getting right on its own.

t: "Speaking Truth to Power" Is Bad Epistemology
q: The ethos of speaking truth to power encourages intellectuals to think that such truths have been established before inquiry has even begun. It replaces a difficult epistemic task — finding out what is true, where power lies, and how truth and power interact in specific cases — with the simpler, more self-flattering goal of summoning intellectual courage.

Intellectuals' primary responsibility is simply to seek and speak the truth, full stop. This job description is less heroic, but it's more intellectually and socially useful, and it's less vulnerable to self-deception precisely because it's less heroic.

In the face of these challenges, large segments of the left-wing intelligentsia and commentariat have coalesced around a simple viewpoint: that AI is basically a nothingburger, a 'con'; that state-of-the-art large language models are little better than 'fancy autocomplete' or 'stochastic parrots'; and that anyone who claims otherwise, including experts who have long worried that AI is extremely dangerous, is simply part of an elaborate propaganda machine.

A totalising hermeneutics of suspicion directed towards 'power' and 'dominant institutions' is no better than high-IQ conspiracy theorising: it simplifies complex realities, flattens important distinctions, and protects itself against refutation by dismissing all criticisms as predictable responses from those in power.

Once one identifies with this self-image, isolated demands for rigour no longer seem like a failure of rigour. They look like bravery. Courageous, truth-seeking intellectuals doubt the powerful; only cowards and apologists for power doubt the powerless.

Mightn't the ethos itself function as a kind of legitimising myth, a way of dressing up activity often rooted in grubby motives — self-aggrandisement, status competition, demonising rivals, and so on — in suspiciously noble clothing?
If we should be highly suspicious of power and its self-serving propaganda, why do intellectuals expend so little effort turning this suspicion inwards on ourselves?

t: The Reality of Understanding
q: Education is full of claims about things we cannot directly see. We say that a child understands fractions. We say that another has a misconception about the equals sign. We say that a class is fluent with multiplication facts, or that they cannot transfer what they have learned to a new context.

The performance is visible. The underlying capacity may not be. Gilbert Ryle made a similar distinction between reciting multiplication facts and calculating them: the same answer can conceal different capacities.

Deutsch's point, as I understand it, is not that every abstraction we invent is real. Many abstractions are confused, dispensable or false. His point is that abstractions are real when they are part of our best explanations. They do not float outside the physical world. They matter because, when instantiated in physical systems, they help explain and change what happens.

The fact that understanding is not directly visible does not make it unreal. The fact that a misconception cannot be pointed to like a chair does not make it fictional. The question is whether these abstractions help explain patterns of learner behaviour better than the alternatives.

Assessment is not direct inspection of learning. It is the design of evidence from which we infer something about learning. Fluency, understanding and transfer are not simply names for test-score bands. They are explanatory hypotheses about the learner.

The problem with educational measurement is not that learning is invisible. It is that many different invisible things can cast the same visible shadow. Good assessment is the attempt to make those shadows diverge.

t: The Either-Or Trap
q: The human brain, faced with a world that is increasingly complex—chock-full of ambiguity and competing priorities and situations that resist any kind of clean resolution—reaches instinctively for the simplicity of two options. Two options are manageable, while a spectrum of choices produces profound tension.

There are managers who decide quickly that a new employee 'gets it' or doesn't (usually within the first few weeks, often on the basis of relatively sparse evidence), thus making a binary call that will surely inform how much investment, opportunity, and developmental feedback that person receives moving forward.

Once I started looking for binary thinking in organizations, I began to uncover it in a lot of different places. For example, I found it encoded in language, embedded in processes, institutionalized in policies, and captured in diverging stances across teams.

From my perspective, the most interesting thing about dichotomous patterns in organizational behavior is that they become so hardened that people feel totally and utterly dictated by ways of seeing and doing that they themselves didn't choose.

When we frame decisions as either-or, we foreclose the both-and options that often turn out to be more generative than either pole can offer on its own. In the spirit of statistical analysis, when we write binary policies, we create systems that fit the average case reasonably well but serve the edges of the distribution poorly, which is often where transformative talent and opportunity live.

I'm not proposing that we eliminate binary thinking, because that's neither possible nor entirely desirable. What I am suggesting is the practice of noticing—of developing enough self-awareness to catch ourselves in moments of harmful bifurcation.

t: Teaching on Purpose #5: Live Modelling
q: Live modelling refers to the teacher building up a model or example piece by piece in the moment, narrating their thought process as they go. Some teachers do this on a board or flip chart while others model onto paper under a visualiser so that the model is projected onto the board for students to see.

By chunking the model into these three component stages, students get to focus on one stage at a time, understanding how it prepares the ground for the next stage of the process and how each stage builds on the previous one.

When we pick up on the fact that students are not following our live model, an adaptation to the planned technique is necessary. Noureddine describes this as being about focusing student attention on the specific part of the model that has caused the confusion—the point in the process where understanding was lost.

Continuing with the pre-planned live modelling process would not be in the best interests of learning because students' misunderstanding of the word would have undermined their understanding of the interpretation of the quote that the teacher was modelling. When there is crucial knowledge that students need to have in place in order to access new learning, teachers need to make sure that that knowledge is in place before continuing, even if this means adapting away from a pre-planned technique.

This approach to live modelling might be well suited to a situation in which students are new to a text or to the convention of annotating quotations. The unfamiliar nature of the content or the task means that learning is well served by explicitly modelling the process so that the steps are replicable and logical.

When students know the content well and are familiar with the process, teachers might decide to ask them to complete the activity independently or in groups first before then comparing their work to a completed exemplar.

t: Reading Aloud Is Not a Soft Option
q: If reading aloud is seen as a lovely thing to do, but not a central part of curriculum work, then it will always be vulnerable. Vulnerable to being squeezed out, to being replaced by another task, or to the idea that 'proper learning' lies elsewhere. But reading to pupils is not a soft option and it's not a pause from learning. It is learning.

When pupils hear rich texts read aloud, they are given access to vocabulary, syntax, knowledge and ideas that they may not yet be able to manage independently. They hear how complex language works. They encounter words in context. They build background knowledge. They experience the rhythm and structure of disciplinary language.

Literacy across the curriculum is not about every teacher becoming an English teacher. It is about every teacher recognising that pupils cannot think deeply in a subject if they cannot access its language.

This is particularly important for pupils who do not arrive at school with large reserves of vocabulary, background knowledge and reading experience. For these pupils, the curriculum has to do more of the heavy lifting.
Reading aloud, shared reading, careful vocabulary teaching and purposeful writing are not extras. They are part of the route into the curriculum.

t: Planning for Emergence
q: Much of what sits inside a typical school improvement plan assumes a level of predictability that the system simply doesn't offer. Goals are defined. Actions are specified. Success criteria are set. Progress is monitored. It is a necessary structure, but it is built on an assumption that if we do the right things, in the right order, we will produce the intended outcomes. And we know, from experience, that it doesn't quite work like that.

Planning for emergence might hold those same desired outcomes in mind but accepts that they will not unfold in a predictable sequence. It recognises that actions are interpreted and adapted as the team goes about its work, with improvements emerging from the interaction between people, ideas and context.

If improvement emerges through patterns of interaction and interpretation, then planning needs to create the conditions in which better patterns are more likely. And what are these conditions? Trusting relationships, intellectual capacity of individuals, organisational capacity to learn.

The role of the leader is fundamentally different if the system is complex, not complicated. If cause and effect are distant, the task is to sustain attention on what is emerging. If systems push back, the task is to adapt in response to how the system is behaving. If small changes can produce large effects, the task is to notice leverage opportunities.

Spend less time perfecting documents (though they still matter for governance and accountability) and spend more time strengthening shared understanding. Spend less time on tracking whether actions are completed (but this is still important) and spend more time on whether thinking is improving.
The real work happens in how people interpret that plan, how they interact with each other in response to it, and how those interactions shape what actually changes.

t: Novels Tell Us Who We Are
q: This, I think, is what novels are for. Not, in some abstract sense, to tell us who we are, the way self-help and personality tests pretend to, but something rarer and stranger. To hand back to us experiences we have been unable to articulate ourselves, sometimes for years, sometimes for a lifetime, in the shape of someone else's sentences.

Language, as Heidegger insisted, is the house of being, the room in which a feeling becomes available to thought. Without the words, the experience drifts in some vestibular space below cognition, still real, still present, but not quite had.
The experience happens to you, but you cannot inhabit it. At its best, I think the novel restores the experience by at least naming it, and in naming it, gives you back to yourself.

What saddens me about our current reading culture is not simply that people are reading fewer books. t: Weekly Top Five: The Particular Forms Us. The Abstract Thins Us.
q: Where is a human being actually formed? Not in the abstraction, not in the program, not in the dashboard, but in the particular: the particular book, the particular place, the particular conversation, the particular struggle that no algorithm can register. That question runs quietly beneath the most serious writing this week.

A child who learns to talk about belief learns to hold belief. Attendance without conversation is presence without formation, and a tradition that cannot be discussed inside its own families is a tradition already losing its grip on the next generation.

The piece matters because it undermines a widely repeated story about masculinity, biology, and behavior that has been doing cultural work it was never qualified to do. t: The Three R's: Revise, Revise, Revise Education Joel
q: What is the aim of this revision? Is it as simple as providing them with information they need to pass, or is it that they need more and more practice in order to be successful? Why do we need a teacher there at all when the students can do this themselves?

The cynic in me would say many schools/teachers run revision, not for the students, but for themselves. It makes us feel better, it makes us think we have given them everything, it makes us believe that we have given them a fighting chance to achieve.

By providing a revision session for pupils, we risk the students becoming reliant on the teacher for said revision. This over reliance means that when it comes to the actual exam, and you are not there, they do not perform as well as they would have if they had completed the revision by themselves.

What we want is pupils to want to do their revision because they want to do well. There are teachers up and down the country who are doing more for their pupil's revision than the pupils are. This is surely not the ideal.

We took down as many barriers as we possibly could to ensure they could revise for themselves. They came to us, all year, and asked for resources. They found us in the corridors to ask us questions. They decided what their revision should look like.

The best antidote for leaders is action. When leaders take a concrete step to address the cause of their anxiety, they reclaim their control and momentum. Purposeful action steadies the mind and builds confidence.

q: I had prepared not a theory, but a system forged through thirteen years of watching empathy fail in high-stakes technical environments. Now with a name, The PACE System was ready for the stage.
