The committee had since dissolved, and no remedy was offered. They oddly noted they 'wanted to be transparent.' Transparency would have been a notification in June 2025, when the recording was lost, not nine months later, when I asked.

Pause: I did not react the day I found out. I sat with it. I separated out what was permanently lost from what remained intact. I organized my records into a Dropbox. The credential was real. The talk happened. The framework existed independently of the video. The pause was not inaction, but the first move.
Pause. Ask. Consider. Empathize. The system I introduced on that stage is the exact system I used when the stage failed me. I did not plan that. But I will not pretend it isn't a proof of concept.

TEDx events are independently organized under license from TED. The brand is only as good as the local committee. This is not a criticism of TED. It is an explanation of the structure. Before you say yes to a TEDx event or really any event where you are giving your time: ask your organizer directly how they plan to fulfill the recording requirement.

t: Promoted to Fail: The Hidden Trap Behind Every Well-Deserved Promotion (The Peter Principle) Leadership
q: The Peter Principle was introduced by Dr. Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull in their 1969 book of the same name. The idea is deceptively simple: In a hierarchy, every employee tends to rise to their level of incompetence.

Here's what often gets missed. The Peter Principle isn't really about the people. It's about the logic of promotion itself. We promote people based on what they've already done -- their past performance in their current role. But the next role is fundamentally different. It demands different skills, different thinking, and different behavior.

The skills that drive individual performance, such as deep technical expertise, focused execution, and personal accountability, are often the opposite of what's needed in a leadership role: delegation, tolerating ambiguity, influencing without authority, and thinking in systems rather than tasks.

When someone struggles after a promotion, the blame lands on them. We say that they weren't ready, or they couldn't handle it. But the real question to ask is: Who decided they were ready? Who prepared them for it? Who supported them through the transition?

The individual loses confidence. Someone who was once a star performer now feels like they're in over their head, every single day. That creates a persistent self-doubt that leaves a mark in their confidence and motivation.
The Peter Principle is a leadership problem, not a people problem. And that means it's yours to solve.

t: Is Ownership the Best Metaphor for Learning? Education Potkalitsky, Nick
q: Ownership is not a neutral word. It carries a logic -- the logic of property. You own something when it passes from outside you to inside you, when it becomes yours. Ownership implies a transaction, a moment of transfer, a before and after.

This is how a constructivist intention ends up producing a retention-based measure. The word ownership sounds like it is describing something the learner does. It is actually describing something the learner gets. The metaphor overrides the intention, quietly and almost invisibly, every time it is used.

The problem is not that the student failed to own the work. The problem is that ownership was never the right frame. What is missing is not possession. It is process -- the cognitive work that produces durable, flexible, actionable knowledge.

Students who used an unguarded AI tutor performed well during practice, then scored 17% worse than students who had never used AI at all once access was removed. They had the answers. They did not have the learning.
Formation is a better word than ownership. You are not the same after genuine learning as you were before. You see differently, reason differently, act differently. That is what the work is for.

Students who generate before they delegate carry something into the AI interaction that changes its character entirely. They have something to think with. Without that prior generation, AI doesn't augment thinking. It replaces it.

What determines which pathway a learner takes is mostly design -- the tools available, the tasks assigned, the evidence gathered. Purpose-built tools structure the interaction around the cognitive work of the discipline rather than the satisfaction of the prompt.

q: Human beings are shaped pre-reflectively through embodiment, relationships, language, ritual, and culture long before they are able to articulate beliefs about themselves or the world. Whether in school exam results or comparisons of lifestyles on TikTok, it becomes clear that being ordinary is not enough. The results are visible. We humans are always already formed through language, education, institutions, media, and relationships. This is not a failure of freedom. It is the condition through which meaning and freedom become possible. The self is not prior to formation but emerges through it.
The question, then, is not whether technology shapes us. It always will. The question is whether we can consciously and collectively take responsibility for shaping the culture that shapes us.

Used well, AI could help education recover what modern institutions have partly lost. AI tutors, moderators, and social platforms could instead be designed to reward curiosity, listening, intellectual humility, courage in questioning assumptions, collaborative problem-solving, and sustained inquiry.

t: Coaching Cut #50: Skipping Success Criteria Leadership Cognitive Coaching
q: Skipping the success criteria is where you model without priming your teacher for what they are about to see. When a coach says, 'I'm going to model this for you, so watch carefully and tell me what you think,' it Page 1 feels like enough. It sounds like an invitation to pay attention. But it's actually a vague instruction.

The coachee is watching everything and focusing on nothing. Their attention lands on whatever is most obvious, the surface features of the technique. The subtler success criteria -- the ones that actually make the practice work -- go unnoticed.

The result is that the coachee rehearses and implements a partial version of the practice. It doesn't have the intended effect on learning, and neither coach nor coachee can easily see why because they never pinned down and verbalised the success criteria that made the technique work.

We wrap the success criteria around the model: before, during, and after. Before the model, we tell the coachee exactly what to watch for. Not everything, just the criteria that matter most, especially any that are subtle or easy to miss.

After the model, we spotlight the key criteria and ask the coachee to explain why they matter for learning. This is where understanding is built. It's not enough that they saw it. They need to understand why it works.

q: The question was raised in the last five minutes of our orals presentation, where we had to convince our client we were the right partner for their $9M technology transformation. The procurement lead leaned forward and said, almost conversationally: We liked your approach, but in order for us to move faster we need an additional discount. Can you do that?

He did what a lot of smart, experienced people do when a new variable enters late: he defaulted to expertise. He talked about how the pricing already reflected the maximum discount, how the scope had been carefully considered, how the value justified the rate. He was not wrong, but he was answering a different question to the one that had just been asked.

What the client read between the lines was that the team struggled to re-orient fast. It is the ability to make sense of information conveyed in written language -- the ability to negotiate the affordances and barriers of text. This is an active reader kind of definition. It includes understanding, inferring, judging, interpreting, relating, and remembering.

I find exercise to be tiring, sweaty, and often boring. I have often fantasized about hiring someone to do those things for me. Cyndie, my wife, is a bit of a killjoy. She is steadfast in her belief that I will have to do my own exercise if I am to benefit.
It is the same when it comes to learning to read. No one else can do that for you -- not even machines that have consumed hundreds of billions of words.

Despite their value for predicting how well kids will comprehend text, readability schemes have been lousy guides for text revision. The issue is whether shortening a few sentences and swapping out some vocabulary improves anybody's comprehension. Over the years, studies have usually said, no.
The revised sentence seems easier. But it fails to convey the same information, a problem that has plagued some efforts to use AI to produce readable health documents.

t: When Peers Strongly Disagree About a Decision
q: There's a difference between disagreeing with a decision — or struggling with its implications — and being unable to live with it. Not being able to live with a peer's decision carries symbolic meaning for the relationship.
When a peer says they can't live with a decision, they are, in essence, saying that making such a choice will indeed create a conflict between the two parties. It is a line in the sand.

Most peers understand the implications of such a statement and refrain from using it unless they feel they must. By calling the question, the decision-maker learns just how important this issue is to their colleague.

In those rare cases when a colleague throws down the gauntlet and says they can't live with a decision, the decision-maker now knows exactly where they stand — and the stakes. The next move is up to them: stand down, continue to negotiate, or make the decision knowing full well that a relational conflict now exists.

Too many peers make a decision that their colleagues are strongly against, creating a nasty conflict that could have been avoided. By asking the question, the decision-maker clarifies the peer's conviction and can now work through the consequences with clear eyes.

Peers who choose not to escalate — who acknowledge they don't like the decision but can live with it — find the question itself thoughtful, respectful, and affirming the relationship. For peers with a good history of collaboration, this is the most common outcome.

t: What Skinner, Criminology, and a Year 9 Boy Taught Me About Behaviour
q: 'I do it for the teachers who actually give detentions.' Not the teachers who shouted the most. Not the ones who gave dramatic speeches. Not even the ones he liked. The teachers who changed his behaviour were the ones who followed through consistently.

Once unpredictability enters the system, behaviour becomes a calculation: 'Will this teacher follow it up?' 'Can I get away with this today?' 'Does this consequence actually happen?' The issue isn't compassion. The issue is unpredictability.
Predictable consequences strengthen behaviour. Inconsistent consequences create unstable behaviour patterns. Unpredictable reinforcement leads to confusion, resistance, and erratic responses.

Countries with extremely high speeding fines (like Switzerland) do not necessarily have lower speeding rates. What does reduce speeding is the presence of average-speed cameras, because drivers know they will be caught. The fine itself is not the deterrent. The certainty of detection is.

Daniel Nagin's 2013 review of decades of deterrence studies showed that people change their behaviour when they believe a consequence is certain, not when it is harsh. Severity has surprisingly little effect unless people think the punishment will actually happen.
Consequences are not about dominance or humiliation. They are about clarity. Predictable environments create psychological safety, fairness, stability, reduced anxiety, and clearer expectations.

Compassion and consistency are not opposites. Students need both. Where schools sometimes go wrong is trying to show compassion through inconsistency. Ironically, this often creates more confusion and stress for the very students we want to support.
Students do not rise to the level of the threat; they adapt to the consistency of the system.

The EBLI multisyllabic split-word reading and spelling strategies helped my student recognize common spelling patterns that developed his accuracy when reading multisyllabic words. The EBLI oral reading practice strategies helped him develop his accuracy and fluency when reading grade level text.

The daily goal setting gave him a concrete goal that showed him what he was aiming for and feedback that motivated him to improve. Seeing his daily success and growth toward his goal empowered him to keep improving.

My biggest takeaway: If something isn't working, don't be afraid to bring in something new. All three resources -- Reading Mastery, EBLI, and Precision Teaching -- are valuable on their own, but combined, they are very powerful in helping a student become a successful reader.

I see a child that came to me barely able to decode, paralyzed by an unknown word, with no skills to break down the word, and minimal confidence in his reading ability, transformed into a confident reader. He is reading grade level chapter books and vocabulary. He's reading out loud in class. He's happy and proud.

t: What Education Can Learn From Trusted Professions
q: At present, education does not function as an evidence-aligned profession. That does not mean it lacks research, talented educators, or worthy intentions. It means the field has not yet built the accountability 'guardrails' needed to make reliable knowledge normal, expected, and enforceable in daily practice.
The period of preventable harm can be defined as the interval of time between when evidence was established and when evidence was uniformly applied by the profession.

In education, local preference too often overrides the strongest available evidence. A teacher may know what works, but the district may prohibit it. A principal may support sound instruction, but a board or superintendent may reverse it. A preparation program may improve, but local curriculum decisions may disconnect new teachers from what they learned.

A hospital cannot say, 'In our clinic, we do not believe in sterile technique.' An accounting office cannot say, 'We prefer not to follow accepted reporting standards.' A ship captain cannot say, 'Our local approach does not include standard navigation or safety procedures.'

The important point, however, is not that these professions have eliminated noncompliance. The important point is that they have built systems strong enough that the shared knowledge base still governs the field overall.

From the beginning of NAEP reading assessments in 1970 through 2024, the United States likely exposed roughly 60 to 70 million fourth graders to unnecessary serious reading failure, if one assumes that the current 'Below Basic' rate of about 40% could have been reduced to 5% to 10% through more effective evidence-based instruction.

That estimate is rough, but its implications are not. It suggests massive preventable harm in the form of reduced confidence, shame, frustration, and anxiety for children; heavy tutoring, advocacy, and emotional burdens for families.

Education still struggles to earn the same kind of trust that states extend to medicine, finance, and maritime work. Why? Effective support for educators and their students is lacking, which disempowers educators and causes widespread student failure.

t: Waiting for Permission
q: I first heard this term when I attended the 1st Annual National Hybrid Schools Project Conference in 2022. I'll admit—I was skeptical. Maybe it's my conservative Southern Baptist upbringing… or my West Coast mentality...where one must ask for permission from the government for pretty much everything.
I remember hearing the term come up multiple times after the conference as well from well-known voices like Kerry McDonald and Don Soifer and thinking, 'We'll see….'

Fast forward to April 2026 where, after a two-year hiatus of my own, I again attended the National Hybrid Schools Project Conference—the 5th annual. I already knew 'permissionless education' was catching on in part due to my own work with new founders and the fact that it was increasing—not decreasing. I was pleasantly surprised, however, to see at the conference just how much the movement is growing and how established these programs are becoming.

Robert shifted gears to home in on the permissionless elements that we are confronted with daily in this space. At one point, Robert said, 'Policy is always backward facing…' and that stuck with me…and apparently others as another attendee, Heidi Fritz from Heart Christian Academy, brought it up to me again last week—commenting that his statement stuck with her as well.
Their response was along the lines of 'You're not a school…you're not a church…we don't know what to do with you…' Sounds familiar!

A mouthful! They apologized for confusion and approved the exemption request.

I have a handful of founders that I am working with in Kansas and I am documenting this particular case so that we can use it as the precedent for other nonprofits requesting exemption in the near future. And just like that…the policy is backward facing.

q: Leaving school isn't just removing something from your child's life -- it's stepping out of a structure that has been organizing their days for years.

t: Pre-Questions and the Attention Advantage
q: Before getting into pre-questions, it's worth grounding this in core idea: attention is the gatekeeper of learning.

Information from the environment first hits sensory memory. From there, only a small portion moves into working memory and the mechanism that determines what gets through is attention. If students don't attend to information, it doesn't matter how well it's explained or how important or relevant it is. It simply doesn't enter working memory in a usable way.

As students move through the FASE text, they're tasked with finding the answers to the pre-questions by underlining or highlighting the relevant information and updating their estimates on their whiteboards. That simple move changes how they approached the text. Because now, they're looking for something.
Students aren't passively moving through the text. They're actively scanning, tracking, and checking. They read more carefully around key details because they don't want to miss the answer.

In the days that follow, during retrieval practice, discussions, and assessments, the information tied to those pre-questions tends to stick more than information not explicitly connected to the questions. Students often remember both the correct answer and their original estimate. That contrast seems to matter.
Realizing I thought it was 15, but it was actually 7 creates a kind of cognitive friction that seems to strengthen their memory.
They move reading from something students complete to something they pursue. And if attention is the gatekeeper of learning, that's not a small impact.

t: If Private Equity Can't Model Five Years Out, How Can a Sixteen-Year-Old?
q: The most sophisticated capital allocators on earth—people who employ armies of analysts, who can pay for any consultant, who have direct relationships with the AI labs themselves—are openly admitting they cannot model what the world looks like in 4 years.
We are asking sixteen-year-olds to make a more confident forecast about the labor market than Blackstone is willing to make about its own portfolio.

When a student gets the bet wrong, there is no portfolio. There is one life, four years, the opportunity cost of those years, and—often—debt that follows them for decades. The 'exit multiple' they're trying to model is their own first job.
The advice sounds prudent. The advice may be catastrophic. And the people giving it have no way to know which.

The educational system refuses to admit it doesn't know. Walk into almost any high school in America, and you'll find the same machinery still running: course catalogs organized around traditional career pathways, guidance counselors steering students toward 'stable' professions, AP tracks designed to feed pre-med and pre-law and pre-business pipelines.
We are sending them toward destinations that may not exist when they arrive, and the system is pretending otherwise.

A student who can think well, evaluate evidence, and defend ideas under cross-examination has a portable capacity that survives any specific economic configuration. A student who has memorized the 2026 marketing curriculum does not.
We are lowballing the only thing we know is durable, while we keep dressing up the things we don't know in the costume of certainty.

t: How Retrieval Practice Changed My Teaching
q: Our first month centered around the Science of Learning, specifically on retrieval practice. I sat there listening, thinking to myself, This is so seemingly obvious, easy to implement, and high impact… so why wasn't I doing it?

I realized that despite all my experience and knowledge, I wasn't consistently using the best evidence-based practices to support how the brain actually learns. And I decided to change that the very next day.

The next morning, I looked at my curriculum and identified moments where I could stop telling and start asking. Some of this even just came to me on the spot. Instead of me standing at the front summarizing what we learned yesterday, I asked them to pull that information out of their own heads.
Positive effects started occurring almost immediately. Learning was sticking in long term memory.

It took me back to one of my favorite college courses—The Psychology of Learning. It all felt so full circle. This is how science has proven the brain learns best. When you realize how low the barrier to entry is for these strategies, it makes you wonder why we aren't all teaching this way by default.

The feedback from other teachers was the most rewarding part. They loved that it wasn't another 'overwhelming PD' full of things we don't have the time or capacity to actually do. It was just real, manageable changes that actually work.

Seeing the impact in my own classroom has been a game-changer. It's a reminder that we don't always need to reinvent the wheel; evidence based practices exist for a reason, and sometimes the tiniest change can make the biggest difference.

q: BERA is getting itself into an awful mess. Two weeks ago, it began the process of retracting papers following my discovery of many, many AI-authored papers in its four journals.

BERA is trying to issue retractions while insisting that it is in the right and I am in the wrong. Everyone that I count on and everyone that I pay needs to be held at arms length, so that I can sue them, drop them, write a one star review, or not feel betrayed by them in case something goes wrong.

q: The problem with this scenario is that despite the teacher providing students feedback on their answers, students are not applying the feedback to their own work. It becomes a classroom version of the question: 'If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound?'

Tick-trick is a system that allows students to apply teacher feedback to their mini whiteboard responses. Once students show you their initial answers, you provide students feedback by asking them to 'tick' the correct components of their work.

Notice that the teacher is using their body language to scan the room. You want to use your body language to communicate to students that you care about what they have written on their mini whiteboards. To communicate this, make sure to exaggerate your movements when scanning the room.

t: Swallowing Our Pride and Turning to the Experts
q: The best way to know if someone is a good teacher is to sit in their room and watch them teach... That's what makes evaluations from our students so valuable. They saw us teach over one-hundred-and-fifty lessons. They spent thousands of minutes in our classrooms. They are the foremost experts on whether or not we are good teachers.

The fear of getting brutally honest feedback from the people who have spent more time in our classroom than anyone else can be paralyzing. But cutting ourselves off from this feedback denies us the most meaningful critiques we could ever receive.

Every year that I asked students to complete an end-of-year evaluation, I got at least some feedback that genuinely hurt. This was far from fun, but nothing improved my craft more than being willing to accept honest critiques from my students.

If you can't give out an evaluation this June, then prepare one to give out next June. This gives you a three-hundred-and-sixty-five-day head start. Knowing what questions your students will answer next June can guide your teaching next September through May.

Instead of 'Teacher cares about the well-being of students,' I used, 'Mr. G cares about me and my well-being.' Instead of 'Teacher presents the subject matter in a way that makes sense,' I used, 'I am able to understand the lesson when Mr. G is teaching the class.'

Do you agree with the following statement? 'If I had the option, I would choose (insert teacher's name) to teach one of my classes next year.' This one question can tell us more about our teaching than a five-page teacher observation rubric.
The answer is sitting in front of us each June. We just need to be willing to ask.

t: I Used to Say 'I Have a Bad Memory' but Now I Know It Was Just Untrained
q: For most of my life, I called this a personal flaw. I have a bad memory. I said it the way some people say I'm bad at math. I used it as half excuse, and half self-diagnosis, fully in the victim mode of I can't change anything about this.

In a 2017 study published in Neuron, researchers worked with a set of people who had no memory training, no special talent, and put them through six weeks of method-of-loci practice. Their word recall more than doubled, from an average of 26 words to 62 out of 72.

Working memory is the small, temporary workspace you use when information is new, unorganized, and not yet connected to anything you already know. It's why a random string like 8-3-1-9-4-0-2-6 vanishes the moment someone interrupts you.
The other part is long-term memory and it works very different from your short-term memory. Its capacity is close to unlimited and the more you learn the more you can remember.

Cognitive scientists call this trap the fluency illusion. The page is doing the remembering for you, and your brain mistakes recognition for recall. You read the line, and think you got it. But when you need the idea later -- for example at the dinner party -- the source isn't there and you wonder why you 'knew it yesterday' but you can't recall it today.

Roediger and Karpicke ran the most-cited version of this experiment. In their 2006 experiment, students studied prose passages and either restudied them or practiced free recall. When tested after a very short delay, restudying looked better. But after longer delays -- especially a week -- retrieval practice led to substantially better retention.

Stop re-reading. Start retrieving, for example, through a spaced repetition system. After you read something, close the source. Try to write down what you remember. Then check. Try to recall the argument. Then go back and look. The act of pulling -- straining, getting it half-right, finding the gap -- is how you build a stronger memory trace.

t: Your Life Expands as You Become More Yourself
q: Real expansion does not begin when our lives get bigger. It begins when we become more fully ourselves.

So much of what surrounds us pulls us away from ourselves. The pace of life, the pressure to perform, the confusion within our systems, the endless noise of reaction, all of it extends an invitation to abandon our center.
To ghost ourselves is to abandon our knowing in order to preserve belonging. It is to mute what is true in us so we can remain comfortable in environments that cannot hold truth.
Leadership begins the moment we decide to end that pattern.

Speaking truth is not blaming. It is not demonizing. It is not strengthening division in the name of righteousness. Real leadership brings truth in a way that opens movement. It reveals where agreement already lives, where cognitive dissonance is blocking progress, and where the next best step might be taken in genuine service to the whole.

When you are rooted in your nature, you are less easily moved by fear. When you trust your Gift, you are less likely to contort yourself for approval. When you know who you are, you are less willing to hand your voice to systems that depend on silence, distortion, or obedience.

The world does not need a perfected version of you. It needs your real presence. This is where expansion begins. Not in becoming better than you are. But in becoming less divided from what is already true.

t: What Your Six-Year-Old Learns About Math With a Pair of Knitting Needles
q: Every knitter is counting constantly. Cast-on stitches. Rows completed. Pattern repeats. They track where they are and where they're going. They hold a number in their head while their hands keep moving, then check it when they finish the row.

When a child makes an error in knitting, the error is visible. Right there in the yarn, three rows back, is a dropped stitch or a wrong count. The work itself becomes the feedback system. Your child doesn't wait to be told they got something wrong. They can see it.
A wrong answer on a math worksheet gets an X. The child turns the page, closes the book, and disengages. A mistake in knitting gets found, examined, and corrected — by the child, on their own terms.

When the only feedback is a grade on a paper they'll never look at again, it's hard for your kid to stay with the work. Knitting works differently. Count wrong and the row is off. Lose track of your pattern and the colors don't land where you expected.

Most of us were taught to equate learning with measurable performance on paper. A grade meant you knew the thing. No grade, or a bad one, meant you didn't. That equation doesn't just disappear when we become parents. It shapes how we read our children's days.

Your child just spent two hours managing numbers, catching errors, adjusting their approach, and finishing something real. They stayed with something long enough to see it through. None of that shows up as a number on a piece of paper.
The math is part of the work. The consequence of getting it wrong is visible. The satisfaction of getting it right belongs to your child.

t: The Moment Before the Moment
q: This is the moment before the moment. We have built almost no language for this interval. We have language for what comes before it: the preparation, the rehearsal, the agenda. We have language for what comes after: the words, the response, the outcome. The narrow window between, where perception happens and direction is chosen, has stayed mostly nameless.

We rehearse our reply while the other person is still talking. We arrive at the meeting already knowing what we're going to say. We walk into the room with the script we built on the drive over, and we run it whether the room calls for it or not. Most failed conversations don't fail at the words. They fail in the moment before the words.

She opens to the room that is actually present, not the room she prepared for in the car. The deal closes. Her colleagues will say she has good instincts. They will say she reads the room. What they mean is they have no idea what she did, but it worked.

What is actually here? Not what you assumed was here or what their words seem to suggest. Not even what the meeting invite said the meeting was about. What is actually present in this moment, in this person's face, in the pace of their breathing, in the energy of the room.

Joe pauses for one half-second longer than is comfortable. In that half-second, he asks himself the question that has saved him more deals than any technique he was ever taught. What is actually here?

Empathy is a feeling; the resonance you experience when you sense someone else's state. The skill that operates in this interval is upstream of feeling. It is perception. It is cognitive. It is the act of seeing what is in front of you, including the parts of what is in front of you that the other person is not announcing.

The other person feels it before they can name it. They feel — actually feel, in their nervous system — that they are being seen, not by a script, not by a trained response, but by another human being who is looking at the actual them, in the actual moment, with no rehearsal between.

t: How Much Practice Do Students Need?
q: Cognitive scientists delineate two different types of memory strength: retrieval strength and storage strength. When you first learn something, retrieval strength is high.

t: Do It for the Kids — and the Adults, Too
q: Most school culture systems fail in the same way. They are designed for one human and burden the other.

The design move that makes the difference is the one most schools never make. The student culture system serves two humans, not one, and its job is to design experiences that reinforce each other rather than compete.

The student needs a safe, predictable, affirming environment in order to learn. The adult needs clarity about what is expected, the tools to deliver it, and the support when the work is hard. Both. At the same time. In the same architecture.
The student experience: I left the room and then I came back. The adult experience: someone made a decision somewhere that I am now living with. Neither person was served. Both were burdened.

Designed for both, the first days of school are a sequence in which the student is taught the school's expectations through demonstration and practice while the adult is rehearsing the correction language, the consequence sequence, and the praise protocols on the same days.

This is what is meant by designing in relationship. Not designing six separate culture subsystems and hoping they fit together. Designing each one with both humans named explicitly, mapped honestly, and held in tension until the design serves them both.

The design move is to refuse the false choice. To build for both humans at once. To accept that culture is not something you do to students with adults as the enforcement layer, and not something you do for adults with students as the input.

t: Article Archive: Leadership The Year Nobody Saw
q: What most people don't understand about shutting something down is that the shutdown isn't the hard part. What follows you is.

Things tried to move it. Emotion tried to move it. The part of me that wanted everyone to feel okay about how it ended tried to move it. The instinct to keep going just a little longer, to do just a little more, to soothe the stomach ache by proving I had done everything possible — that tried to move it too.

The mistake people make is thinking empathy requires self-sacrifice. It doesn't. Empathy is 'I understand this hurts.' A boundary is 'and this is still the reality.' Most people won't like that those two things can coexist. The reality doesn't serve them. But it has to be said anyway because the alternative is you absorbing consequences that were never yours to carry.

What kept me on the line was not willpower. It was people. My husband. My therapist. A handful of entrepreneurs who had been through something like this not once but multiple times. They had the outside perspective I couldn't manufacture for myself.

Support isn't a luxury. It's not something you earn once you've proven you can handle things alone. It's the thing that makes handling things actually possible. All the time. But especially in the moments when you can't see clearly and someone who loves you can.
x: The central insight is that shutting something down is not the hard part; what follows the decision is.

The year that produces trust in yourself is often the year no one sees — the one where you held something difficult while building something new at the same time.

t: Article Archive: Family Why So Many Young Men Can't Carry Weight
q: Young men are not collapsing under pressure. Most have never been trained to carry it.

For most of human history, boys did not drift into adulthood. They were brought into it through expectation, pressure, and example. They were given responsibility before they felt ready, corrected when they failed, and surrounded by older men who embodied the standards they were expected to meet.

When a boy grows up without a father, he does not simply lose a relationship. He loses the most consistent and influential source of male formation available to him. He loses the daily observation of what it looks like to work, to persist, to restrain impulses, and to take responsibility for others when it is inconvenient or costly.

Freedom detached from responsibility does not produce strength. It produces drift. In that environment, young men do what human beings reliably do when structure disappears. They default to what is immediately rewarding. Comfort takes precedence over challenge, entertainment over effort, and avoidance over responsibility.

A young man can understand his anxiety and still be unable to act. He can describe his fears in precise language and still refuse responsibility. Insight does not produce strength, and in many cases it produces awareness without movement.

The result is a generation of young men who have been told that they are free but have never been required to become anything in particular. They have been affirmed but not formed, supported but not strengthened.

When young men are placed in environments where something real is expected of them, they tend to respond. Responsibility, when paired with guidance, has a clarifying effect. It forces decisions, exposes weakness, and creates the conditions under which growth becomes necessary rather than optional.

t: AI in Education #6: Five Things I Learned from Dan Meyer about Why AI Should Serve Teachers, Not Replace Them
q: If you have ever sat beside a student and helped them through a problem, you know the decisions involved are constant and subtle. When do you intervene? When do you hold back? When does a student need encouragement, and when do they need to be told: “No, keep going, you are closer than you think”? These are not just cognitive decisions. They are social ones.

Dan pointed to Khanmigo’s struggle with something as basic as when to offer help. First, they had it off until the student clicked it. Nobody clicked. Then they triggered it when a student clicked into the answer box and clicked out. Now it is just always on. These are the largest companies in ed-tech, and they cannot solve the timing problem.
The AI does the language processing. The teacher does the work of building relationships around mathematical content.

Dan put it bluntly: Students do not care about bringing their best work to an AI chatbot. They do care about their classmates seeing them. They care when the teacher says, "Ooh, this is wrong, but very interesting." That has an effect — socially, on every single person in the classroom.

If you analyse the efficacy reports from personalised learning companies – the ones that claim their AI tutoring platform produces measurable gains - you typically find that the positive results only emerge after excluding what appears to be 90–95% of the study population. The students who did not engage enough, who did not complete enough sessions, who dropped out.

If the technology only works for 5% of students, that still leaves 95% unserved. And the 5% it works for are likely the students who were already most motivated and most capable of self-directed learning.

Relative to other technological innovations – the steam engine, the combustion engine, vaccinations, the telegraph – AI has not yet transformed the day-to-day experience of most people. It is, as Dan put it, all potential energy and no kinetic.

Dan’s hypothesis: the success of AI would generate value for a small number of people who have a lot of interest in both media properties and AI companies. And so it does not surprise him that the media talks about AI quite a lot, and that people like you and me, further downstream, find ourselves talking about it too – instead of talking about the social and political solutions that are harder but more likely to work.

t: The Questions You Won't Ask
q: You’ll question anything, as long as it threatens your point of view. But you’ll protect anything that reinforces your self-image.
The challenge is not that they question things. The challenge is that they are so certain of their beliefs, they stop questioning.

In the group debrief, the VP blamed the market because market conditions had changed. He blamed the team because they didn’t execute the way he thought they should. He blamed the timeline because the strategy would’ve worked if they had just a little more runway. The only thing the VP didn’t blame in that meeting was the strategy itself.

Your brain does the exact same thing. You’ll remember the wins that validate your business prowess and forget the losses that question it. Consciously or not, you are always looking for evidence to confirm what you already believe and you’ll dismiss the evidence that contradicts it.

q: It is possible to interrogate the phrases to shed light on which interpretation is correct: are the phrases indicative of LLM-generated text (not allowed) or are they indicative of LLM polishing and summarising existing author-written text (allowed). It is again possible, at least in theory, that thousands of scholars wrote this specific idea but were unhappy with the wording, and so had LLMs polish it, but it is much more likely that this is just a standard LLM phrase that appears when LLMs are used to generate text describing research.

BERA’s glib assertion that the use of phrases that exploded in popularity since 2023 is not a sign of LLM-generated text does not stand up to scrutiny. t: The Libero Leader
q: In volleyball, the Libero is the player spectators almost never notice — until they have a deeper understanding of the game. The Libero doesn't spike, doesn't block, and can't rotate to the front row. The role exists entirely in the service of others.

The Libero reads the play before it develops, absorbs pressure in the backcourt, and creates the conditions for the hitters to swing freely. Even though they are typically the team's best passers and diggers, they receive little fanfare, glory, or attention.

This isn't servant leadership. It's more about facilitation than passive support. More about strategic coordination than driving to outcomes. Libero leaders simply guide and position people to succeed more than they direct or control.

Becoming the best leader you can be comes down to your willingness to put people and winning above self-interest. When you do, anything is possible.

t: The Bridge and the Novel: What Humanities Departments Never Told You About Yourself
q: You are teaching your student to take a text they have never seen before, decompose it into its constituent components, understand how those components interact under pressure, identify where the argument or the narrative is doing its most important work, propose an interpretation, and defend that interpretation against competing readings. The claim I want to make explicit is this: literary analysis and engineering are not two different kinds of thinking applied to different problems. They are the same underlying cognitive process — what we might call the decomposition-connection-extension loop — applied to different substrates.

What AI does, structurally, is collapse the distance between intent and implementation. The bottleneck in a growing class of problems is no longer execution — writing the code, querying the database, building the pipeline. These tasks are increasingly handled at the AI layer. The bottleneck shifts upstream, to the work that precedes execution: correctly characterizing the problem, decomposing it into its components, understanding the relationships that matter, anticipating second-order consequences, and producing a coherent claim about what should be built and why.

Comfort with ambiguity. Literary training insists that you sit with a text that does not resolve cleanly, that resists your first interpretation, that contains genuine tension between competing readings. You are not rewarded for forcing premature closure. You are rewarded for holding the ambiguity long enough to say something true about it. This is exactly the disposition required when working on problems where the parameters are unstable and the requirements are incompletely specified — which describes most real organizational problems.

t: How Smart Leaders Use Language to Create Clarity
q: Clarity is the oxygen of high-performing organizations and teams. Without clarity, people pull in different directions and quietly drift away from the foundations of mission, vision, and values. Clarity drives results.
The job of clarity is one of translation — making sure the leader's understanding survives contact with the reality that team members experience. Language plays a critical role in this translation.

Words matter to leaders who want to create clarity. That's why the best leaders and organizations are obsessively precise about the labels, titles, and names they use for technology, products, processes, and initiatives — and anything else of importance.

Inconsistent language feels minor but quietly creates a stew of confusion and complexity. When leaders and team members use different words to describe anything of importance, teams spend a surprising amount of time just translating each other's meaning instead of moving forward.

Words aren't just labels. They shape how people think. When everyone agrees on what terms like 'strategy,' 'end user,' 'deadline,' and 'customer' mean, the team operates from the same internal map. Without that shared understanding, two team members can agree but still be imagining completely different outcomes.

When leaders don't insist that words, names, and labels remain uniform, people naturally introduce their own descriptors, which then create noise and confusion. So good leaders not only give everything of importance a specific title or name, but they also insist that everyone else do the same.

q: The five-paragraph essay fits this stable Victorian noetic field like a glove. It assumes that the writer has the thesis before drafting begins; that the thesis describes a state of affairs that exists out there to be retrieved; that paragraphs are containers carrying that thesis from writer to reader without alteration; and that the audience reading the essay is being served, not joined.

Berlin in the 1980s saw one possible future for writing by studying the distant past set in motion by a little known 19th century Scottish psychologist. There would be a real struggle to humanize writing instruction which would challenge the five-paragraph essay tradition.
We are teaching a way of experiencing the world, a way of ordering and making sense of it.
The paragraph is not just a structural unit, but a metaphysics transmitted as procedure—and because it is enacted rather than taught, it does not require defenders. It requires only practitioners.

The five-paragraph essay is not a tradition; it is a revenant, an undead being. Its noetic field died sometime in the second half of the twentieth century, killed by linguistics, phenomenology, the cognitive revolution, and the New Rhetoric.

t: 5 Ridiculously Simple Management Moves That Shouldn't Work (But Do)
q: Some of the highest-impact management moves are almost embarrassingly simple. So simple, in fact, that most managers overlook them, not because they're ineffective, but because they feel too basic to matter.
The managers who consistently outperform others aren't always the smartest or the most experienced, but the ones who do the obvious things consistently, and well.

Most managers feel the pressure to have answers. So when someone brings up a problem, the instinct is to solve it, direct it, or fix it. But try this instead: ask them: 'What do you think?' And then, just wait. Don't jump in after two seconds of silence, or lead the answer, nudge them in any way. Just wait.
Without [the Owner/Action/Timeline structure], meetings create the illusion of progress. With it, they drive real meaning and momentum.

When you say 'I don't know,' you actually build trust, not lose it, because people are smart and good at detecting when something doesn't feel authentic. Leaders who acknowledge what they don't know signal that it's safe to speak up, question, and explore.

Individually, these moments don't feel like much, but over time, they compound, and what they're really signaling is: 'I notice. I remember. I care.' And that builds helps you to build lasting trust with your team.

When you look closely, they all drive the same three outcomes: Clarity — People know what's expected. Ownership — People feel responsible for outcomes. Trust — People feel heard and supported. And those three things are the foundation of every high-performing team.

t: 3-Read Friday #109: Gradual Release, Attainment Setting, and Atomisation
q: Regular readers will know I love nothing more than a bit of I Do, We Do, You Do.

Here, Mark Enser argues that gradual release only works when teachers genuinely release -- making expert thinking visible at each stage and accepting that productive struggle, not extended scaffolding, is the point at which learning actually begins.
I am going to do a deep dive into this week's EEF report into mixed attainment setting in mathematics in Monday's Research Bites newsletter.

But in the meantime, the fantastic Becky Allen argues that the evidence now closes the setting debate in maths -- setting helps high attainers and harms no group -- but also exposes the deeper, neglected problem that low-attaining pupils have heterogeneous needs that no grouping policy, only specialised diagnosis and intervention, can address.

Kris shows, through loads of concrete examples, that Atomisation lets teachers identify and focus instruction on only the genuinely new atoms in a cognitive routine -- wherever they sit in the chain -- building deep conceptual mastery before students ever attempt the full process end to end.
